patient_actor_hidden.History: The patient reports experiencing fever, chills, and a headache starting three days after undergoing an open cholecystectomy. She has a history of an abdominal hysterectomy 16 years ago. She has been smoking one pack of cigarettes daily for 17 years.

Symptoms.Primary_Symptom: Right-sided chest pain that increases on inspiration
Secondary_Symptoms: Productive cough for the last 12 hours

Social_History.Smoking_Status: Current smoker, one pack daily for 17 years

Review_of_Systems.Gastrointestinal: Surgical site below right ribcage, otherwise unremarkable

objective_for_doctor: Evaluate the patient presenting with postoperative fever, chest pain that increases on inspiration, and a productive cough, and determine the correct diagnosis.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, what brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had fever and chills with a headache, and I’m also having right-sided chest pain that gets worse when I breathe in. I have a productive cough that started within the last day, and this all began a few days after my open cholecystectomy.
Doctor: Have you noticed any shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, especially when you’re lying flat?

Patient: I do feel more short of breath when I move around, but I haven’t noticed any trouble breathing when I lie flat. My breathing also feels a bit limited because the right-sided chest pain gets worse when I take a deep breath.
Doctor: Have you noticed any swelling, pain, or tenderness in your legs—especially in the calves—since your surgery?
Patient: No, I haven’t noticed any swelling, redness, or tenderness in my legs or calves since the surgery.
Doctor: Can you describe the sputum you’re coughing up—its color, consistency, and whether it’s foul‑smelling?
Patient: The sputum is yellowish and fairly thick, not watery, and it doesn’t seem especially foul‑smelling. It’s been coming up since the cough started about 12 hours ago.
Doctor: What is your current temperature, and have you measured it at home or here in the emergency department?
Doctor, I haven’t measured my temperature at home, but here it was about 38.5°C. I’ve been feeling feverish and having chills since the symptoms started a few days after my surgery.
Doctor: What is your current respiratory rate and oxygen saturation on room air?

Patient: I don’t know my exact respiratory rate, but I’ve been breathing faster because taking a deep breath hurts on the right side. My oxygen saturation on room air was low enough to make me feel a bit more short of breath when I’m moving, but I don’t recall the exact number.

Doctor: Can you describe the chest pain in more detail—how would you rate its intensity (0‑10), is it sharp or dull, does it stay in one spot or radiate elsewhere, and does anything (like coughing or movement) make it better or worse?

Patient: The pain is pretty sharp, about an 8 out of 10, and it stays on the right side of my chest without really moving anywhere else. It’s definitely worse when I take a deep breath or cough, and it doesn’t feel any better with rest.
Doctor: What are your current heart rate and blood pressure, or have you had any episodes of feeling light‑headed, palpitations, or faintness?

Patient: I don’t know my heart rate or blood pressure, and I haven’t felt faint or light-headed. I also haven’t noticed palpitations. I’ve just been mostly limited because the sharp right-sided pain gets worse when I breathe in.
Doctor: When was your cholecystectomy performed, and were you given any blood‑thinners (e.g., low‑dose heparin or enoxaparin) for clot prevention after the surgery?
Patient: The open cholecystectomy was three days ago. I’m not sure whether I was given any blood-thinners for clot prevention after the surgery—I didn’t notice any.
Doctor: On exam of your lungs, do you hear any crackles, wheezes, or a pleural friction rub on the right side, and is there any dullness to percussion over that area?

Patient: I haven’t been able to tell you exactly what the doctors heard, but when I take a deep breath it’s very painful on the right. I don’t notice wheezing, and I haven’t felt any rubbing sensation on the chest.
Doctor: Since your surgery three days ago, have you been able to get out of bed and walk around, or have you been mostly confined to bed rest?
Patient: I’ve been mostly confined to bed, and I’ve only gotten up briefly to use the bathroom. When I try to move around, my shortness of breath and the sharp right-sided chest pain get worse.
Doctor: Have you coughed up any blood or noticed any pink‑tinged sputum?
Patient: No, I haven’t coughed up any blood, and the sputum hasn’t been pink-tinged—just yellowish and thick.
Doctor: Do you have a history of smoking or any chronic lung conditions such as asthma or COPD?
Patient: I’ve been smoking about a pack a day for roughly 17 years, but I don’t have any known asthma or COPD. I haven’t been on any inhalers or breathing treatments.
Doctor: On exam of your lungs, do you notice any decreased breath sounds, crackles, or other abnormal sounds over the right side, especially in the lower zones?

Patient: I can’t say what decreased breath sounds or crackles you’re hearing over the right side because I mainly just feel the sharp pain when I breathe deep. I haven’t noticed any wheezing myself, and moving around seems to make the right-sided pain and shortness of breath worse.
Doctor: Have you had a chest X‑ray (or any imaging of your lungs) since these symptoms began, and if so, what did the report say?
Patient: I haven’t had a chest X‑ray or any lung imaging since these symptoms started.
[DDX] Postoperative bacterial pneumonia, Pulmonary embolism, Post‑operative atelectasis, Parapneumonic pleural effusion/empyema, Acute pericarditis (post‑surgical)
